newsitem.title: USA: U.S. utilities doubt customers will shop for power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. utilities doubt customers will shop for power.

text.p: U.S. utilities widely expect their markets to be open to competition soon, but doubt that all their customers will shop around for power when given the choice, according to a survey released Wednesday by the Washington International Energy Group.
In 557 responses to a survey of 4,235 U.S. and Canadian utility executives, 86 percent said customer choice was inevitable, up from 63 percent a year ago, the private consulting group said.
But only 43 percent believed that their customers would take advantage of direct access to power suppliers.

John Anderson, executive director of the Electric Consumers Resources Council, representing big industries, said oversubscription to pilot programs for open power supply choice in states such as New Hampshire suggested otherwise.
Contrary to what advocates of competition say, only 12 percent of the executives believed that the average family would see sharply lower electric bills in an open market.

The consulting group itself predicted that in the short term, "customers in some low-price service areas are likely to see increased bills as aggressive marketers create broad regional equilibrium prices."
There was no consensus on whether competition among utilities would harm the environment.
About 36 percent of the executives said it would result in more pollution, 45 percent said it would not, and 20 percent said they were not sure.
But the consulting group said in the long run competition should help the environment by encouraging innovation.
With mergers proliferating, half the executives said their companies would not remain intact in the next 10 years.
Among investor-owned utilities, 56 percent predicted they would merge or be taken over.
Washington International Energy Group president Roger Gale said the white gloves would come off in the industry in 1997 as the prospect of competition spawned hostile takeovers.
"Finally, we are begining to see the facade of civility cracking," he said at a news conference.
In the 1997 survey, 87 percent of executives said they expected electric utilities would merge with gas utilities, up from 64 percent in the survey a year ago.
And 66 percent said they expected electric utilities would merge with telecommunications companies, compared with 57 percent who predicted the same in last year's survey.
